title: Emergency alerts
keywords: Read an alert for place, time, hazard and action
Build several warning routes with different weaknesses
Configure the device and local service deliberately
Match each warning to the correct protective plan
Make warning access work during sleep and impairment
Keep the plan usable when alerts are absent or conflicting
tldr: Check an official alert for your exact location, hazard, timing and required action. Enable emergency alerts on your phone and add local emergency management notifications. Keep a battery radio as backup rather than relying on one app.
steps: Review emergency notification settings and keep the phone charged.
Sign up with your county or city emergency management office and utility.
For weather hazards, use NOAA Weather Radio or your local official warning service.
Distinguish preparation notices from instructions to shelter or evacuate.
next: Write down local frequencies and contact information. Test devices and accessibility features with your household.
watch: Alerts can be delayed or missed. Act on obvious immediate danger and natural warning signs.
review_status: source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
without_help: Treat direct signs of danger as a reason to act even if an alert has not arrived. Compare a battery-radio bulletin with another independently obtained source when possible. Record the place and time; an old screenshot can be dangerously misleading.
household: Check how each person notices and understands warnings, including while sleeping. Assign assistance and a backup, and use suitable visual, vibration, language or communication support where needed.
pack_now: A charged compatible phone, local notification details, configured weather receiver with suitable backup, any supported accessible alert equipment and a short hazard-response card.
faqs: Do I need an app for U.S. Wireless Emergency Alerts?

NWS describes WEA delivery through compatible participating mobile service without an app subscription. Check current phone and carrier support; a separate app or local signup may cover other information.
Does no alert mean no danger?
No. A channel can fail or not cover a particular event. Act on obvious immediate danger and use the relevant protective plan and another working information route.
scope: Civilian educational guidance. Linked references may use U.S. emergency systems; local warning methods, laws, services and conditions differ.

sections.heading: Read an alert for place, time, hazard and action

blocks.text: An alert is useful when you can tell whether it applies to you and what to do next. Read the affected location, issue time, hazard, required action, and issuing organization. An old screenshot, a warning for the next county, or a storm headline without an action can cause the wrong response. Do not let searching for extra detail delay a clear instruction to protect yourself.

blocks.caption: Turn an alert into an action
items: Does the named area include where you are now, not only your home address?
What hazard, timing and protective action does the message describe?
Carry out the applicable instruction and use a working source for subsequent updates.
blocks.note: Editorial planning aid. Actual hazards, individual needs and current instructions control the response.

blocks.text: Editorial example: a family visiting another town needs information for that town as well as the home they left. Keep names of counties, local places, and accommodation addresses available. If an alert uses an unfamiliar zone, verify the location against the local system in advance; do not assume a flood zone, evacuation zone, and warning area are interchangeable.

sections.heading: Build several warning routes with different weaknesses

blocks.text: A phone, a broadcast receiver, and a local notification service can complement one another. Multiple apps on one uncharged phone still share the same device and power failure. List what each route covers, how it is powered, and who can perceive it. Include warning arrangements at work, school, a campground, or another regular location, rather than limiting the plan to the living room.

blocks.text: No single channel covers every kind of incident. A weather receiver is not a household smoke alarm, and an email utility notice may not arrive quickly enough for an immediate hazard. Record a backup that serves the particular need instead of collecting notification services without checking their function.

sections.heading: Configure the device and local service deliberately

blocks.text: Use the phone and carrier’s current instructions to check supported emergency alert settings. Separate those settings from an app’s notifications and a city’s subscription list. The NWS describes U.S. Wireless Emergency Alerts as messages delivered through participating mobile service without needing an app subscription. That does not establish that every phone, location, or hazard will generate an alert.

items: Find the local emergency management subscription from an independently obtained official address, rather than a forwarded signup link.
Select the relevant places and delivery methods. Review saved addresses after moving or changing work locations.
Check that a telephone number or email address was entered correctly and complete any legitimate confirmation process.
Review language and accessibility options, and teach another adult where the settings are.
Check current device behavior for mute, focus, notifications and power settings using its instructions; do not assume every alarm bypasses every mode.

blocks.text: A successful signup is only the beginning. If the service offers a documented test or sample message, use that procedure. Do not contact emergency dispatch to ask whether an app notification works.

sections.heading: Match each warning to the correct protective plan

blocks.text: The same loud sound may introduce very different hazards. Keep a short response card with the household’s relevant shelter spaces, departure arrangements, and care tasks. Use the current message and hazard-specific guide. A generic instruction to “go downstairs” can be unsuitable for some flooding or chemical incidents; a generic instruction to “go outside” can also place people in danger.

blocks.caption: A response card is more useful than a list of alert names
rows: Immediate building escape
Usable exits, dependent assistance and a safe outside accounting point.
Tornado protection
The appropriate sturdy shelter and how to reach it safely.
Regional evacuation
The affected location, transport, checked destination and route.
Hazard-specific sheltering
The correct space and any ventilation instructions for that incident.

blocks.text: Define tasks that can happen together: one adult reads the action aloud while another supports a child or dependent person. If alone, put the essential instruction and reachable equipment in one familiar place. Do not make verification of a message a lengthy voting process when direct danger is already apparent.

sections.heading: Make warning access work during sleep and impairment

blocks.text: A warning nobody notices cannot support the plan. Check the actual sleeping arrangement, normal door positions, hearing and vision needs, and whether someone uses headphones or assistive communication. For supported weather receivers, compatible visual or vibration equipment may help. Verify the full system, including power to any attachment, through its manufacturer’s documented procedure.

blocks.title: Volume alone is not an accessibility plan
blocks.text: Ask the person what presentation they can reliably perceive and understand. An adult assigned to wake them also needs a backup if away, asleep elsewhere, or unable to help.

Write a plain-language interpretation for household members who may not understand the alert language or technical terms. Use agreed words such as the named room or destination instead of vague calls to “get ready.” Do not promise that any device guarantees waking everyone, and do not test alarms in a way that creates injury, panic, or unnecessary distress.

sections.heading: Keep the plan usable when alerts are absent or conflicting

blocks.text: A missing alert does not establish safety. Act on obvious immediate danger and the relevant natural warning signs. If two reports appear to conflict, compare issue times, locations, hazards, and source identity from a safe place. The later report may apply elsewhere, or one may be an old repost. Keep observations, verified instructions, and rumors separate in a short note.

items: Record the exact location and time of the message you are using.
Carry out any applicable immediate protective instruction.
Use another available warning route for updates without abandoning necessary protection.
Tell the household what has changed and what remains unknown.
Change the plan when credible new information or actual conditions require it.
Afterward, review missed alerts, configuration and assistance needs.

blocks.text: Do not treat silence from a receiver or a phone as an all-clear. A dead battery, weak signal, or transmitter problem can look like a quiet day. Once conditions allow, inspect the failed channel and repair the cause. Keep the written response card current so a technical fault does not also erase the household’s knowledge of what to do.
